title: AI Unlocked: Public Health
blurb: For public health professionals and institutions: surveillance and outbreak analytics, health communication at population scale, program M&E, supply-chain intelligence, and governance — informed by real national-institute systems work with Africa CDC.

modules.t: AI Across the Public Health Cycle
modules.d: Where AI adds value at every stage — surveillance, analysis, response, communication, and evaluation.
modules.body:
Public health is an information discipline — which makes it an AI discipline

At its core, public health is about turning data into decisions that protect populations: spotting threats early, understanding them, acting, communicating, and learning. Every one of those steps is information work — and every one is amplified by AI. This module maps where AI adds value across the full public health cycle so you can see the whole landscape before going deep. Your judgment, ethics, and community knowledge remain the irreplaceable core; AI is the force-multiplier.

"The greatest public health tool has always been information moving faster than the threat." From John Snow's cholera map to today's outbreak dashboards, the discipline advances when we see and understand faster. AI is the newest, most powerful accelerant — in the hands of professionals who know its limits.

The public health cycle, with AI at every stage

  • Surveillance & early detection: AI scans diverse data — clinical reports, search trends, news, lab feeds — to flag emerging signals faster than manual monitoring. Earlier detection saves lives.
  • Analysis & understanding: AI helps analyze epidemiological data, model spread, identify risk factors, and summarize evidence (Module 1). It turns raw numbers into insight.
  • Response & programs: AI supports planning, resource allocation, and logistics — who needs what, where, and when (Module 3).
  • Communication: AI drafts clear, multilingual, culturally-appropriate health messages at population scale — a superpower for reach (Module 2).
  • Monitoring & evaluation (M&E): AI accelerates data cleaning, indicator tracking, and reporting so programs learn and improve (Module 3).

The non-negotiables (Commandments, applied to public health)

  • Human expertise decides. AI informs; epidemiologists, clinicians, and public health officials decide. A wrong call at population scale harms many — verification is vital (Commandment 2).
  • Data protection is sacred. Health data is deeply sensitive. Never expose identifiable patient or population data to non-approved tools (Module 4 goes deep). Do no harm.
  • Equity is the goal, not an afterthought. AI can widen or narrow health gaps depending on how it's used. Public health AI must actively serve the underserved (Module 4).
  • Context matters. A model trained elsewhere may not fit your population. Local knowledge validates every AI output.
Regional relevance: for institutions like national public health agencies and NPHIs across Africa and beyond, AI is especially powerful where resources are stretched — doing the work of a larger team on surveillance, analysis, and communication. But the same resource constraints make governance and data protection more important, not less. This course balances capability with responsibility throughout.

Going deeper — lessons from real deployments

Public health AI has a track record worth learning from, both successes and cautionary tales.

  • Early warning works when paired with people: systems such as HealthMap, BlueDot and the WHO's Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS) scan news and reports to flag unusual events. Their value comes from human epidemiologists verifying signals before action.
  • Google Flu Trends overestimated flu activity substantially in 2012–13 because search behaviour changed while the model didn't — a classic lesson in data drift and in validating against ground truth.
  • Population algorithms can encode inequity: a widely used US care-management algorithm (Obermeyer et al., 2019) used health spending as a proxy for health need, so it underestimated the needs of Black patients who had less access to care. The proxy, not the maths, caused the bias.
Map the cycle before choosing tools: surveillance → analysis → communication → programmes and supply → monitoring and evaluation → policy. For each stage ask: what decision does it support, what data feeds it, who verifies outputs, and who could be harmed if it's wrong?
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a public health informatics adviser. For [my institution and country], map the public health cycle stages, and for each give one realistic AI use case, the data it needs, the decision it supports, who verifies outputs, the equity risk, and whether the data currently exists in usable form.

📚 Glossary

  • Event-based surveillance: Detecting outbreaks from news, reports and informal sources
  • Data drift: Change in underlying data patterns that degrades a model
  • Proxy variable: A measurable stand-in for something harder to measure
  • EIOS: WHO Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources

📖 References

  • Lazer, D. et al. (2014). The parable of Google Flu: traps in big data analysis. Science.
  • Obermeyer, Z. et al. (2019). Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations. Science.
  • WHO — Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS).

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • See the whole cycle. AI helps at every stage — map your own work to surveillance, analysis, response, communication, or M&E.
  • Governance scales with resource constraints. The leaner the team, the more discipline data protection needs.
  • Local context validates everything. A model built elsewhere may not fit your population — always check.

📚 Glossary

  • Surveillance: ongoing monitoring to detect health threats.
  • Epidemiology: the study of how disease spreads in populations.
  • M&E: monitoring and evaluation of programs.
  • NPHI: National Public Health Institute.

📖 Explore further

  • WHO — Ethics & governance of AI for health.
  • Africa CDC — continental public health leadership.

quiz.q: At 07:00 an event-based surveillance tool at Cameroon's NPHI flags radio and WhatsApp reports of five deaths after a funeral in a rural district of the East Region. What should the duty officer do first?
opts: The clinics under-reported cases, so the model is probably nearer the truth
Ask the district team to verify the reports and gather case details today
Wait for the weekly DHIS2 report to confirm the signal before reacting
Ask the AI tool to estimate case numbers and send that to the ministry
quiz.x: Event-based signals are meant to be verified by people before action, so calling the district team comes first. An immediate public alert is the runner-up instinct, but an unverified alert can cause panic and erode trust.

quiz.q: A Kenyan county team built a flu-activity model on internet search volumes. It tracked well for two years, then began reporting roughly double the clinic-confirmed influenza-like illness. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: A genuinely larger epidemic started that clinics have not yet detected
The clinics under-reported cases, so the model is probably closer to truth
Search behaviour shifted while the model stayed fixed, so it drifted
The model was too small and needs more parameters to fit the new season
quiz.x: This mirrors Google Flu Trends in 2012-13: behaviour changed but the model did not (data drift), so it must be revalidated against ground truth. Assuming clinic under-reporting is the tempting runner-up, but it trusts the proxy over the confirmed data.

quiz.q: A US health system bought a care-management algorithm that ranks patients by predicted future health spending. An audit finds Black patients with the same illness burden get lower scores. What is the root cause?
opts: Spending was used as a proxy for need, and less access meant less spending
The audit sample was too small to draw conclusions about any subgroup
Race was included as an input variable and should simply be removed from it
The model's statistics were faulty and would be fixed by retraining it
quiz.x: As Obermeyer et al. (2019) showed, the proxy (spending) rather than the maths caused the bias, because unequal access lowers spending. Removing a race variable sounds right but leaves the biased proxy in place.

quiz.q: A regional delegation in Garoua wants an AI tool to estimate how a measles outbreak in one district might spread to neighbouring districts over the next month. Which stage of the public health cycle is this?
opts: Surveillance and early detection of new health signals
Monitoring and evaluation of programme indicators
Communication of risk and protective action to the public
Analysis and understanding of spread and risk factors
quiz.x: Modelling spread is analysis and understanding. Surveillance is the runner-up because the data comes from surveillance, but detecting a signal is different from modelling how it will evolve.

quiz.q: A lean NPHI team of six in Chad argues that, because they are short-staffed, they can relax data-protection reviews to get AI tools working faster. How does the module view this?
opts: Agree for aggregate data, but keep the reviews for line-level patient records
Agree, since speed of capability matters most for small teams
Lean teams need more governance discipline, not less, to stay safe
Defer the decision to the tool vendor's own data-protection terms
quiz.x: The module says resource constraints make governance and data protection more important, not less. Relaxing reviews for aggregate data is a defensible-sounding runner-up, but small cells in aggregates can still re-identify people.

quiz.q: A WHO-style open-source intelligence system flags 40 unusual events in a week across West Africa. Most turn out to be noise. A manager proposes switching it off. What is the strongest response?
opts: Replace it with indicator-based surveillance from clinics alone
Keep it, with epidemiologists triaging and verifying each signal
Switch it off, since frequent false signals erode staff attention
Keep it, but auto-escalate any event mentioned in three sources
quiz.x: Systems like EIOS add value because human epidemiologists verify signals; noise is expected in event-based surveillance. Auto-escalation by source count is the runner-up, but it removes the human verification that gives the system its value.

quiz.q: A partner offers Cameroon's NPHI a malaria risk model trained on data from Southeast Asian health districts, claiming 92% accuracy. What is the most important check before using it in the Adamawa Region?
opts: Validate its performance on local Adamawa data with local experts
Confirm the vendor's 92% accuracy figure with a published study
Compare its price and licence terms with two other vendor models
Check that it runs on the NPHI's existing servers and connectivity
quiz.x: A model trained elsewhere may not fit your population, so local validation with local knowledge comes first. Confirming the published accuracy is the runner-up, but accuracy on another population says little about this one.

quiz.q: A Ghana Health Service officer is mapping AI uses for a strategy note. For each stage she asks what decision it supports and what data feeds it. Which additional pair of questions does the module add?
opts: Which donor will fund it, and when will the pilot results be reported?
Which vendor supplies the tool, and what does the licence cost?
How fast is the model, and how many languages does it support?
Who verifies the outputs, and who could be harmed if it is wrong?
quiz.x: The module's mapping asks what decision it supports, what data feeds it, who verifies outputs and who could be harmed if it is wrong. Cost and vendor questions matter later, but they do not test safety and accountability.

quiz.q: During a cholera response in the Far North, an AI tool drafts a press release stating a 4.1% case fatality rate. The incident manager has 20 minutes before a briefing. What should happen to the figure?
opts: Replace it with the WHO global cholera CFR to stay on safe ground
Trace it to the current line list and confirm it before release
Round it to 'about 4%' so any small error matters less to readers
Publish it, as it can be corrected later if the line list differs
quiz.x: Human expertise decides and every figure must be verified against the source before a population-scale message. Rounding feels prudent but still publishes an unverified number; a global CFR misdescribes the local situation.

quiz.q: A Ministry of Health in Senegal asks a consultant where AI adds most value for a stretched team. Which statement best reflects the module's view of AI's role?
opts: AI multiplies the team's reach while people keep judgment and ethics
AI replaces some epidemiologist posts so funds can move to field work
AI should wait until the team has full data scientists on staff
AI is best kept to communication, where errors carry low stakes
quiz.x: The module frames AI as a force-multiplier across the whole cycle while judgment, ethics and community knowledge stay human. Restricting AI to communication is a cautious runner-up but understates its value and wrongly calls communication low-stakes.

facts.t: John Snow mapped cholera deaths around London's Broad Street pump.
facts.more: His map linked cases to one water source, and the pump handle was removed. Information moving faster than the threat is still the core of public health.

facts.t: Google Flu Trends' overestimate of US flu activity at the 2012–13 peak.
facts.more: Search behaviour changed while the model did not. Lazer et al. (2014) used it as the classic lesson in data drift and validating against ground truth.

facts.t: WHO's Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources scans news and reports for unusual events.
facts.more: Its value comes from epidemiologists verifying each signal before anyone acts. Event-based surveillance flags; people confirm.

facts.t: A US care-management algorithm underestimated Black patients' needs.
facts.more: Obermeyer et al. (2019) found it used health spending as a proxy for need; people with less access spent less. The proxy, not the maths, caused the bias.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the early-warning signal
plaibox.intro: You are a surveillance officer at a national public health institute. An event-based system flags a cluster. Make each call.

steps.s: The system flags social-media posts about several deaths after a funeral in a rural district.
o: Ignore it — social media is unreliable
Event-based signals are exactly how early outbreaks surface; verify, don't dismiss.
Call the district team to verify the signal
Right — human verification of the signal comes first.
Issue a public alert to be safe
Premature; an unverified alert can cause panic and erode trust.

steps.s: The district confirms 6 suspected cases. An AI model forecasts 400 cases in 3 weeks.
o: Use the forecast as one input and ask about its assumptions
Correct — models inform; check assumptions and local fit.
Request the full 400-case response budget now, to be safe
Treating a model output as fact; forecasts carry wide uncertainty.
Disregard the model entirely and rely on field reports
Loses useful planning information; interrogate it instead.

steps.s: A partner offers a free cloud AI tool to analyse the line list with names.
o: Accept; speed matters most in an active outbreak
Identifiable data in a non-approved tool is a breach, even in a crisis.
Use it after removing names, since IDs alone seem harmless
Better, but dates, villages and ages can re-identify in small communities.
Use approved tools or minimised, de-identified data
Right — data protection matters more, not less, under pressure.

steps.s: You must brief the minister tomorrow.
o: Present verified facts, uncertainties and options
AI can draft, but the brief must separate verified facts from uncertainty.
Forward the AI summary unedited to save time
Unverified AI text at ministerial level risks a costly error.
Delay the brief until all district data are complete
Waiting for certainty can cost lives; brief honestly now.

plaibox.win: Excellent: signal verified, model used wisely, data protected, decision-makers informed honestly.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the non-negotiables: human verification, data protection, and AI informs while officials decide.

modules.d: AI as your analyst — explore data, summarize evidence, and model spread, with rigor and verification.
modules.body:
Your tireless research and analysis assistant

Epidemiological work is data- and literature-heavy: cleaning datasets, exploring patterns, reviewing evidence, and modeling. AI accelerates all of it — acting as an analyst who never tires — provided you apply professional rigor and verify everything. This module shows how to get real value while avoiding the traps that make AI dangerous in analysis.

Where AI genuinely helps

  • Data exploration & cleaning: "Here's my dataset structure — suggest cleaning steps, flag likely errors, and propose useful summary statistics." AI speeds the tedious first mile.
  • Explaining methods & code: whether you use R, Python, or a stats package, AI explains methods, drafts analysis code, and debugs it — lowering the technical barrier.
  • Literature synthesis: "Summarize the key findings, methods, and limitations across these studies on [topic]." A first-pass evidence review in minutes — which you then verify against the sources.
  • Plain-language translation: turn complex findings into clear summaries for non-specialists and decision-makers (ties to Module 2).
  • Hypothesis generation: "Given these patterns, what hypotheses might explain them, and how could each be tested?" AI widens your thinking; you judge plausibility.
"AI is a superb research assistant and a terrible authority." Use it to accelerate exploration, drafting, and explanation — never as the final word on a statistical result, a causal claim, or a clinical fact. The analyst's judgment is the authority; the AI is the assistant.

The rigor rules (where analysis goes wrong)

  • Verify every number and citation. AI hallucinates statistics and references convincingly. Trace each to the real source before it informs a decision.
  • Ground it in your data. Give the AI your actual data to reason over (or use grounded tools like NotebookLM) rather than trusting its memory — this is the single biggest accuracy upgrade.
  • Correlation is not causation — and AI will happily blur them. Hold the line on causal reasoning; demand the evidence.
  • Watch for bias in data and model. Ask "whose data is missing? what population does this represent?" — Level 1's GIGO principle at professional stakes.
  • Statistical significance still needs a statistician. AI can compute and explain, but interpretation and study design remain expert territory.
Operator workflow: use AI for the first mile (exploration, cleaning, code, drafts) and the last mile (plain-language summaries), while keeping the middle mile — method choice, interpretation, causal claims — firmly in expert hands. That division captures the speed without ceding the judgment.

🧪 Analysis lab (copy → run with your own data structure)

You are an epidemiological data analyst. Here is my dataset's structure and variables: [describe]. My question: [describe]. Suggest: (1) sensible cleaning steps and likely data-quality issues to check, (2) appropriate descriptive statistics and visualizations, (3) which analytical methods might fit — with their assumptions and limitations. For any statistic or claim, tell me exactly what I must verify myself. Do NOT invent numbers; work only from what I provide.

Going deeper — analytic rigour when AI writes your code

AI can write R, Python or Stata code for cleaning, descriptive analysis and models in seconds. The risks are subtle:

  • Silent data errors: code may drop rows with missing values, mis-parse dates (day/month confusion), or treat codes like 99 (= unknown) as real numbers. Always compare row counts and summary statistics before and after each step.
  • Wrong denominators: rates need correct populations at risk. AI may compute crude rates where age-standardised rates are required for comparison across districts with different age structures.
  • Small numbers: rates from tiny populations are unstable. Report confidence intervals, and suppress or aggregate small cells to protect privacy.
  • Causal overreach: AI write-ups often slip into causal language from observational data. Check every "caused", "led to" and "due to".
Worked example. District A: 30 cases in 10,000 people = 3.0 per 1,000. District B: 6 cases in 1,000 = 6.0 per 1,000. B's rate looks double, but with only 6 cases its 95% confidence interval is wide (roughly 2.2–13.1 per 1,000 using an exact Poisson interval). The difference may be chance. Ask AI to compute the intervals and explain them.

Literature support

AI can speed up evidence summaries, but verify citations, and for formal reviews follow PRISMA and report AI's role.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a senior epidemiologist reviewing my analysis. Here is my AI-generated code and output: [paste]. Check row counts at each step, handling of missing and coded values, date parsing, denominators and whether standardisation is needed, confidence intervals for small numbers, and any causal language not justified by the design.

📚 Glossary

  • Crude rate: Cases divided by total population, unadjusted
  • Age-standardised rate: Rate adjusted to a standard age structure for fair comparison
  • Confidence interval: Range of plausible values for an estimate
  • Small-cell suppression: Hiding counts too small to report safely or reliably

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • First mile and last mile. Let AI accelerate cleaning/code and plain-language summaries; keep interpretation expert-owned.
  • Ground it in your data. Reasoning over your actual data beats trusting the model's memory — the biggest accuracy upgrade.
  • Hold the causal line. AI blurs correlation and causation; demand the evidence.

📚 Glossary

  • Data cleaning: preparing raw data for analysis.
  • Literature synthesis: summarizing findings across studies.
  • Confounding: a hidden factor distorting an apparent relationship.
  • Grounding: having AI reason over provided data/sources, not memory.

📖 Explore further

  • NotebookLM for grounded literature Q&A; general models for code and explanation.
  • Level 2's data-storytelling module pairs perfectly with this analysis work.

quiz.q: District A reports 30 cholera cases in 10,000 people; District B reports 6 cases in 1,000. An AI summary says 'District B has double the risk and needs priority response.' What is the best analyst reaction?
opts: Accept it, because 6.0 per 1,000 is clearly double 3.0 per 1,000
Recompute both rates per 100,000 so the difference becomes much clearer
Check the confidence intervals, since 6 cases give an unstable rate
Reject it, because District A has five times more cases than B
quiz.x: Rates are 3.0 and 6.0 per 1,000, but with 6 cases B's 95% CI is roughly 2.2-13.1 per 1,000, so the difference may be chance. Accepting the doubling is the tempting runner-up because the arithmetic is right; the interpretation is not.

quiz.q: An analyst in Bamenda asks an AI tool to write R code to compute mean age from a survey. The mean comes out at 41 years, though the population is young. Ages coded 99 mean 'unknown'. What most likely happened?
opts: R rounds ages upward when computing means by default
The survey sampled too many older adults in rural areas
The AI used the median instead of the mean by mistake
The code treated 99 as a real age, inflating the mean
quiz.x: Coded values such as 99 = unknown are a classic silent error in AI-written code; check codes and compare summaries before and after each step. Sampling bias is a plausible runner-up but would not usually push the mean this far.

quiz.q: Two districts have identical crude mortality rates, but District X has many more elderly residents than District Y. A programme manager wants to compare their underlying mortality fairly. What should the analysis use?
opts: Crude rates, since the totals already include every age group
Rates per 100,000 instead of per 1,000 for both districts
Age-standardised rates adjusted to a common age structure
The median age at death in each district as the comparison
quiz.x: Age-standardisation removes the effect of different age structures. Equal crude rates with an older X actually suggest Y has higher age-specific mortality. Changing the multiplier to per 100,000 changes nothing about comparability.

quiz.q: A Nigerian epidemiologist pastes 12 study abstracts into an AI tool for a rapid evidence summary for a ministerial brief. The summary cites a 2021 Lancet trial she does not recognise. What should she do?
opts: Trace the citation to its source and drop it if it is not real
Keep it, since the AI was given real abstracts to work from
Keep it but label it 'unverified' in the brief's footnote
Ask the AI whether the citation is real before she includes it in the brief
quiz.x: AI hallucinates references convincingly, so every citation must be traced to the real source. Asking the AI to confirm is the runner-up but the same model can repeat the fabrication; an 'unverified' label still puts it before a minister.

quiz.q: An AI write-up of a cross-sectional survey in Douala says 'poor handwashing led to the rise in diarrhoea cases'. The survey measured both at one point in time. What is the right edit?
opts: Add a reference to a trial elsewhere to justify the causal claim
Delete the finding, since cross-sectional data cannot show anything
Keep 'led to', because the association was statistically significant
Change it to 'was associated with' and note the design's limits
quiz.x: Observational cross-sectional data supports association, not causation, so causal verbs must go. Significance is the runner-up argument, but significance does not establish direction or rule out confounding.

quiz.q: A team at Burkina Faso's NPHI must decide whether a new outbreak investigation should use a cohort or a case-control design. Under the first-mile, middle-mile, last-mile workflow, who owns this choice?
opts: The ministry's communications team, who will present the results
The expert team, with AI explaining options and assumptions
The AI tool, provided a statistician signs off its output later
The AI tool, since it can compare designs faster than people
quiz.x: Method choice is middle-mile work owned by experts; AI can explain options and assumptions. Letting AI choose with later sign-off is the runner-up but cedes the judgment the module keeps with people.

quiz.q: A Ugandan analyst's AI-written script merges two line lists. Before the merge there were 1,240 rows; after, 1,087. No step was meant to drop records. What is the best next action?
opts: Ask the AI to rewrite the merge in Python instead of R
Find which rows dropped and why before any analysis continues
Accept the result, since merges usually remove duplicate rows
Report both counts in a footnote and then continue with the analysis
quiz.x: Comparing row counts at each step is exactly how silent data errors are caught; 153 unexplained losses must be traced. Footnoting both counts is transparent but still lets possibly biased data drive results.

quiz.q: An onset-date field reads '03/04/2026'. An AI cleaning script parsed dates as month/day, but the data was entered day/month. What is the main analytical consequence?
opts: The epidemic curve shifts, as some onsets move by weeks or months
Attack rates rise, because the denominator is recalculated
Case counts fall, because invalid dates are dropped from totals
Nothing material, since all dates shift by the same amount
quiz.x: Day/month confusion moves onset dates (3 April becomes 4 March) and distorts the epidemic curve; check parsed ranges against what is possible. Dropped rows can also occur for days above 12, but the main harm is distorted timing.

quiz.q: A Malawi district reports 4 TB cases in 800 people (5.0 per 1,000). The region reports 40 cases in 20,000 (2.0 per 1,000). A manager wants to publish the district figure in a village-level table. What two concerns apply?
opts: Seasonality, and the need to wait for a full year of reporting
Wrong multiplier, and the need for a per-100,000 rate for the table instead
Age standardisation, and the cost of producing the new table
Instability from small numbers, and possible re-identification
quiz.x: With 4 cases the rate is unstable (report a confidence interval) and small cells can identify individuals, so suppress or aggregate. Age standardisation is a reasonable runner-up concern but does not address either key risk.

quiz.q: A researcher wants an AI tool to answer questions about a set of 30 national surveillance reports. Which approach most improves accuracy, according to the module?
opts: Use the largest general model and ask it to cite its sources
Ask several different chatbots and keep the majority answer
Ground the AI in the uploaded reports and check its answers
Set the model to a low temperature so answers stay consistent
quiz.x: Grounding the AI in your actual sources (for example NotebookLM) is the biggest accuracy upgrade, with checks still required. Asking for citations from memory is the runner-up but can still yield fabricated references.

facts.t: Approximate 95% CI per 1,000 for 6 cases in 1,000 people (exact Poisson).
facts.more: The rate looks double a district with 3.0 per 1,000, but the interval is wide. With small numbers the difference may be chance.

facts.t: A common survey code that AI-written code may treat as a real value.
facts.more: An 'age' of 99 or a 'parity' of 99 can wreck a mean. Check coded and missing values and compare summaries before and after each step.

facts.t: 3 April or 4 March? Date parsing is a silent error source.
facts.more: Day/month confusion shifts onset dates and epidemic curves. Check parsed date ranges against what is possible.

facts.t: Needed to compare districts with different age structures.
facts.more: A district with older residents will have higher crude rates of chronic disease. Standardise before comparing, and ask AI to explain the method it used.

plaibox.intro: Compare two districts. Try District B with 6 cases in 1,000 people, then with 60 in 10,000 — same rate, very different certainty.

modules.d: Clear, trusted, multilingual, culturally-grounded messaging — AI's public health superpower.
modules.body:
The message is the intervention

In public health, the best science fails if people don't understand or trust the message. Communication is the intervention — and it's where AI is a genuine superpower: producing clear, accurate, multilingual, culturally-appropriate messaging at population scale, in a fraction of the usual time. This module shows how to wield it responsibly, because at scale a bad message does bad at scale too.

"Health literacy is a matter of life and death, one message at a time." A vaccine no one trusts, or an alert no one understands, saves no one. AI lets a small team communicate to a whole population, in their languages and on their terms — if the human keeps it accurate and respectful.

Where AI transforms health communication

  • Plain-language translation of complex science: "Rewrite this clinical guidance for a general audience at a basic reading level, warm and non-alarmist." Health literacy, instantly.
  • True multilingual reach: draft messages across the languages your population actually speaks — then have a human speaker review for accuracy and nuance.
  • Cultural adaptation: "Adapt this message for [community], respecting [context/beliefs], avoiding [sensitivities]." Relevance drives uptake.
  • Channel-native versions: one message becomes a radio script, a WhatsApp broadcast, a poster, a social post, an SMS — shaped for each channel your audience uses.
  • Countering misinformation: draft clear, respectful, evidence-based responses to circulating myths — fast, before they spread.
  • Audience-specific messaging: the same guidance tailored for parents, elders, health workers, or youth.

The responsibility rules (scale cuts both ways)

  • Accuracy first, always. A hallucinated health instruction sent to thousands is a serious harm. Every message is verified by a qualified human before release (Commandment 2).
  • Human review for language & culture. AI translation is a draft; a fluent, culturally-grounded person confirms it says what you mean and respects the audience.
  • Trust is fragile. One wrong or tone-deaf message erodes credibility built over years. Respect and dignity are not optional.
  • Match the messenger. AI drafts the words, but trusted local voices deliver them — community leaders, health workers, familiar faces.
Regional superpower: in multilingual, mobile-first settings, AI-drafted messaging across local languages — delivered via WhatsApp, radio, and SMS — lets a lean public health team reach communities that top-down English-only campaigns never touch. Pair AI's speed with human cultural review and trusted local messengers, and reach multiplies without sacrificing trust.

Need
Guidance too technical for the public
Reach speakers of several languages
A dangerous myth is spreading
Same message for radio, WhatsApp, SMS
AI move
Plain-language rewrite

🧪 Communication lab (copy → run for a real message)

You are a public health communication specialist. Take this guidance: [paste the technical message]. Rewrite it for [audience] at a basic reading level — warm, clear, non-alarmist, and culturally respectful of [context]. Then produce channel versions: a short WhatsApp/SMS message, a 30-second radio script, and a poster headline + two lines. Flag anything that MUST be checked by a qualified human and a fluent local speaker before release. Do not alter any medical fact — if unsure, say so.

Going deeper — testing messages before they reach millions

At population scale, a confusing or culturally tone-deaf message does real harm. Professional health communicators use AI to draft quickly, then test with people.

  • Plain language: short sentences, everyday words, one main action. Readability tools help, but the real test is whether your audience can say back what to do.
  • Translation quality: machine translation of health messages can carry meaning errors, especially in less-resourced languages (e.g. Fulfulde, Ewondo, Cameroonian Pidgin). Use back-translation by a fluent speaker and check with community members.
  • Pre-testing: a quick focus group or 10 short interviews checking comprehension, acceptability, relevance and persuasion. Change what confuses people.
  • Infodemic management: WHO describes an infodemic as too much information, including false or misleading information, during an outbreak. Monitor rumours (social listening), respond quickly with clear facts, and work with trusted messengers — health workers, religious and community leaders.
Never let AI invent facts in health messages. Every number, dose, symptom and instruction must match an approved source (national guidelines, WHO). Keep an approval step with a named technical reviewer.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a health communication specialist. Draft a 60-word message on [topic] for [audience] in plain language, with one main action. Then produce a pre-testing plan with five comprehension questions, a back-translation check for [language], and a list of trusted messengers in [community] to deliver it. Flag every fact that must be checked against national guidelines.

📚 Glossary

  • Back-translation: Translating a text back to the original language to check meaning
  • Pre-testing: Testing messages with the target audience before release
  • Infodemic: Overabundance of information, including misinformation, during a health emergency
  • Trusted messenger: A person the audience trusts to deliver information

📖 References

  • WHO — Infodemic management resources and WHO Strategic Communications Framework (2017).
  • CDC — Everyday Words for Public Health Communication.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • AI translation is a draft. Always have a fluent, culturally-grounded human confirm meaning and nuance before release.
  • Match the messenger. Trusted local voices deliver AI-drafted words — credibility lives in the messenger.
  • Scale cuts both ways. Verify every message; a wrong one reaches everyone too.

📚 Glossary

  • Health literacy: people's ability to understand and use health information.
  • Cultural adaptation: tailoring a message to a community's context.
  • Channel-native: shaped for a specific medium (radio, SMS, WhatsApp).
  • Risk communication: conveying threat and action clearly and calmly.

📖 Explore further

  • WHO — health literacy resources.
  • Level 1's media modules and Level 2's brand-voice work strengthen your messaging craft.

quiz.q: Cameroon's NPHI has an AI-drafted cholera prevention SMS in French, English, Fulfulde and Pidgin. The drafts were made from the national guideline. In what order should review steps happen?
opts: Translate first, then check facts in each of the four versions
Check facts against the guideline, then translate and back-translate
Back-translate each version, then have a reviewer check the facts
Pre-test the English draft, then translate it and release all versions
quiz.x: Facts are checked before translation, otherwise errors are translated into every language. Back-translating first is the runner-up: it checks meaning but multiplies the work if the source facts were wrong.

quiz.q: A health communicator in Maroua receives an AI translation of a vaccination message into Fulfulde. A colleague says the AI is 'very good at languages'. What is the right quality step?
opts: Have a fluent speaker back-translate and community members check it
Release it, since modern models translate major African languages well
Shorten the message so that there is less text that could be wrong
Run it through a second AI translator and compare both versions
quiz.x: Machine translation is weakest in less-resourced languages such as Fulfulde, so fluent human back-translation and community checks are needed. A second AI comparison is the runner-up but both tools can share the same errors.

quiz.q: A rumour spreads on WhatsApp in Yaounde that a new vaccine causes infertility. The communications lead has an AI-drafted rebuttal. Which delivery plan best fits the module?
opts: Wait a week to see whether the rumour fades away before responding to it
Post the rebuttal from the ministry account with all the evidence
Reply to each post that repeats the rumour with a link to WHO data
Have trusted health workers and faith leaders share a short, clear reply
quiz.x: Infodemic management calls for fast, clear responses delivered by trusted messengers. A detailed ministry post is the runner-up but credibility lives in the messenger, and dense evidence may not reach the people sharing the rumour.

quiz.q: A team pre-tests a 60-word handwashing radio message with 10 market traders in Douala. Seven can say back the main action; three describe a different action. What should the team do?
opts: Translate it into more languages to reach the remaining 30%
Add a second action so more listeners find something useful
Revise the confusing wording and re-test before release
Release it, since a 70% comprehension rate is acceptable
quiz.x: Pre-testing exists to change what confuses people; if three in ten misread the main action, revise and re-test. Adding a second action is the tempting runner-up but works against the one-main-action rule.

quiz.q: An AI-drafted SMS for a cholera campaign says 'Add 2 capfuls of bleach per litre of water.' The national guideline gives a different amount. The deadline is tonight. What is the right action?
opts: Send it to a small district first to check how people respond
Send it, but add a line advising people to ask a local health worker first
Remove the dosage and tell people to treat water before drinking
Correct it to match the guideline and get named technical sign-off
quiz.x: Every dose and instruction must match an approved source, with a named technical reviewer approving. Removing the dosage is a defensible runner-up but makes the message vague and unusable for the main action.

quiz.q: A US county health department wants the same flu-vaccine guidance for parents, older adults and high-school athletes, delivered by text, radio and Instagram. What is the most efficient AI-assisted approach?
opts: Adapt the verified core message per audience and per channel format
Use the radio script for every channel to keep wording consistent
Write separate guidance for each group from different sources
Write one long message that covers all three groups on every channel
quiz.x: Audience-specific and channel-native versions of one verified core message improve relevance without changing facts. Separate guidance from different sources is the runner-up but risks inconsistent facts across groups.

quiz.q: A Nigerian state campaign has an accurate, fluent AI-drafted message, but uptake is low in one community where the state government is distrusted. What does the module suggest changing first?
opts: The language, switching to English to sound more authoritative
The channel, moving from radio to the state's official website
The messenger, using trusted local leaders and health workers
The wording, making it more urgent so the risk feels real
quiz.x: Match the messenger: credibility lives in trusted local voices. More urgent wording is the runner-up but can feel alarmist and does not fix the trust problem.

quiz.q: A communications officer asks an AI tool to rewrite a technical guideline on oral rehydration for the general public. Which prompt instruction best protects accuracy?
opts: Include as much clinical detail as the guideline contains
Do not alter any medical fact, and say so if you are unsure
Use the latest published research to update the guideline where needed
Make it warm, short and engaging for a basic reading level
quiz.x: The module's prompts tell the AI not to alter any medical fact and to flag uncertainty. Tone instructions are useful but do not protect accuracy; asking for updates invites invented facts.

quiz.q: During an mpox outbreak, an NPHI's social listening finds a fast-growing false claim on Facebook. A staff member suggests waiting until the next weekly bulletin to respond. What does infodemic management advise?
opts: Ask the platform to remove the posts and avoid public comment
Respond quickly with clear, reviewed facts via trusted messengers
Wait for the bulletin, so the response is fully reviewed
Publish a long technical rebuttal on the institute's website
quiz.x: WHO infodemic guidance stresses monitoring and responding quickly with clear facts through trusted messengers; speed and review are both possible. Waiting for the bulletin is the cautious runner-up but lets the myth spread for days.

quiz.q: A team checks an AI-drafted message with a readability tool and gets a basic reading-level score. Is the message ready for release from a plain-language standpoint?
opts: Not yet; test whether the audience can say back what to do
Yes, provided the message stays under 60 words in total length
Yes, since the score confirms the audience can read it
Not yet; run it through two more readability tools first
quiz.x: Readability tools help, but the real test is whether the audience can say back what to do. Extra readability tools are the runner-up but measure text features, not comprehension by real people.

facts.more: An English-only or French-only campaign misses many communities. AI drafts help reach them — but only fluent human review makes them safe.

facts.more: Manage it with social listening, fast clear responses and trusted messengers — health workers, religious and community leaders.

modules.d: AI for planning, resource allocation, monitoring & evaluation, and getting supplies where they're needed.
modules.body:
Turning strategy into delivery

Public health impact happens in delivery: the right program, resourced well, reaching the right people, measured honestly, and improved over time. AI strengthens each link — planning, allocation, logistics, and monitoring & evaluation — especially valuable where budgets and staff are stretched thin. This module maps AI across the operational backbone of public health, with the same rule throughout: AI informs the plan; accountable humans own the decisions.

AI in program planning & resource allocation

  • Needs assessment: "Analyze this district data and summarize the top health needs, the populations most affected, and the gaps in current services." A faster, structured starting point for planning.
  • Resource allocation support: AI helps model where limited resources — staff, funds, supplies — do the most good, surfacing trade-offs for human decision-makers to weigh (Level 2's decision-partner skills apply).
  • Proposal & report drafting: grant proposals, program narratives, and donor reports drafted fast, then refined — reclaiming time for delivery (ties to the NGO specialization).

AI in monitoring & evaluation (M&E)

  • Data cleaning & management: the tedious backbone of M&E — AI accelerates cleaning, coding, and structuring survey and program data.
  • Indicator tracking: summarize progress against targets and flag where a program is off-track and why.
  • Qualitative analysis: "Identify the recurring themes in these open-ended survey responses / interview notes." AI surfaces patterns across large qualitative datasets fast.
  • Reporting: turn M&E data into clear narratives and visuals for stakeholders (Level 2's data storytelling).

AI in supply chain & logistics

  • Demand forecasting: support for anticipating needs for medicines, vaccines, and supplies — reducing both stockouts and waste.
  • Distribution planning: help optimize routing and allocation to get supplies where they're needed, when.
  • Last-mile problem-solving: reason through the local constraints — roads, cold chain, staffing — that make or break delivery.
"A vaccine in a warehouse saves no one; a vaccine in an arm saves a life." The unglamorous work of logistics and M&E is where public health strategy becomes real impact — and where AI quietly earns its keep for stretched teams.
The operator's rule for operations: AI is excellent at analysis, drafting, and surfacing options; it must never own a resource or allocation decision. Health resource decisions carry ethical and equity weight (who gets served, who waits) that requires accountable human judgment. AI informs the plan; a responsible person decides and answers for it.
🧪 Interactive Lab — Match the task to its function
Task
Summarize a district's top health needs
Find themes across open survey responses
Forecast vaccine demand to avoid stockouts
Turn M&E data into a stakeholder narrative
Function
Planning / needs assessment
M&E — qualitative analysis
Supply chain / forecasting
Reporting

🧪 Validated exercise

AI can surface options, but must never OWN a resource or allocation ___.

Going deeper — forecasting, logistics and honest M&E

Supply chain forecasting: AI and statistical models can improve demand forecasts for medicines and commodities, but only if consumption data is reliable. Where stock-outs occurred, recorded consumption understates real demand. Adjust for stock-out days, seasonality and programme changes, and compare forecasts with actual use each month.

  • Data quality first: in many health information systems (e.g. DHIS2), completeness, timeliness and consistency vary. Run data quality checks — outliers, missing reports, internal consistency — before modelling.
  • M&E integrity: AI can draft logframes, indicators and reports quickly. Ensure indicators are SMART, measure outcomes not just activities, and that reports don't overstate results. Donors increasingly spot AI-polished reports with thin evidence.
  • Attribution vs contribution: most programme data can't prove your programme caused change; contribution analysis explains plausibly how it contributed alongside other factors.
Worked stock example. A clinic used 300 units last month but was out of stock for 10 of 30 days. Adjusted demand ≈ 300 × 30 ÷ 20 = 450 units. Ordering on the unadjusted 300 would repeat the stock-out.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a public health supply chain and M&E adviser. Here is my programme's consumption data and indicators: [paste]. Run data quality checks, adjust consumption for stock-out days, propose a forecast with assumptions, and review my indicators: are they SMART, outcome-focused, and honestly reported? Suggest how to describe contribution rather than attribution.

📚 Glossary

  • DHIS2: Widely used open-source health information system
  • Adjusted consumption: Consumption corrected for days out of stock
  • Logframe: Logical framework linking activities, outputs, outcomes and impact
  • Contribution analysis: Explaining how a programme plausibly contributed to change

📖 References

  • WHO (2017). Data quality review: a toolkit for facility data quality assessment.
  • Mayne, J. (2012). Contribution analysis: coming of age? Evaluation.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • AI surfaces options; humans decide. Allocation carries equity weight — keep it accountable.
  • M&E's tedious middle is AI's home turf. Cleaning, coding, and theme-finding are huge time savers.
  • Forecasting cuts both stockouts and waste. Better demand estimates protect supplies and budgets.

📚 Glossary

  • M&E: monitoring and evaluation — tracking and judging program performance.
  • Needs assessment: identifying a population's priority health needs.
  • Demand forecasting: anticipating required quantities of supplies.
  • Last mile: the final, hardest step of getting supplies to people.

📖 Explore further

  • The NGOs & Nonprofits and Procurement specializations deepen program and supply-chain skills.
  • Level 2's decision-partner and data-storytelling modules apply directly here.

quiz.q: A health centre in Bertoua used 240 vials of oxytocin last month but was stocked out for 6 of 30 days. What is the stock-out-adjusted monthly demand?
opts: 320 vials, scaling 240 by 30 divided by 22.5 days
288 vials, adding 20% for the six days out of stock
300 vials, scaling 240 by 30 divided by 24 days in stock
240 vials, as recorded consumption already reflects demand
quiz.x: Adjusted demand = 240 x 30 / (30 - 6) = 300 vials. Adding 20% (288) is the runner-up shortcut, but stock-out days should scale consumption by days available, not by a flat percentage.

quiz.q: A clinic used 450 doses of an antimalarial last month and was out of stock for 15 of 30 days. It holds 300 doses now. Roughly how many months of adjusted demand does the stock on hand cover?
opts: About 2 months, assuming no further stock-outs occur
About 1.5 months, dividing 450 by the 300 doses on hand
About 0.67 months, since recorded use is 450 doses a month
About a third of a month, as true need is near 900 doses
quiz.x: Adjusted demand = 450 x 30 / 15 = 900 doses, so 300 / 900 = 0.33 months. Using recorded use (0.67 months) is the runner-up but overstates cover and would repeat the stock-out.

quiz.q: An NGO in northern Cameroon reports '% of households owning at least one bed net' to show its malaria programme succeeded. Where does this indicator sit in a logframe, per the module's lab?
opts: Impact, because it shows reduced malaria in the region
Activity, because nets were distributed during the campaign
Output, because it shows what the programme delivered
Outcome, because it shows a change in household behaviour
quiz.x: Ownership is an output; sleeping under a net is the outcome. Outcome is the runner-up, but owning a net does not show it was used.

quiz.q: An AI tool ranks 12 districts in the Centre Region for allocating 5,000 extra vaccine doses and recommends sending most to the three easiest to reach. Who should make the final allocation?
opts: The AI tool, since its ranking uses the most data available
The district with the highest demand forecast, by agreement
The donor, since it funded the doses and set the targets
An accountable official who weighs equity and the AI's options
quiz.x: AI may surface options, but allocation carries equity weight and needs an accountable human decision. Following the forecast leader sounds objective but ignores who waits and why.

quiz.q: Before training a demand-forecasting model on three years of DHIS2 facility data, what should a Zambian supply chain team do first?
opts: Collect three more years of data first so the model is more stable
Run data quality checks for completeness, timeliness and outliers
Train the model and let it learn around missing or odd data
Choose the model type that scored best on public benchmarks
quiz.x: DHIS2 completeness, timeliness and consistency vary, so data quality checks come before modelling. More data is the runner-up but adds the same quality problems.

quiz.q: A donor report drafted by AI for a Kenyan maternal health programme says the programme 'reduced maternal deaths by 30%'. The data comes from routine facility records with no comparison group. What is the best revision?
opts: Describe the programme's plausible contribution alongside other factors
Remove the figure and report the number of trainings held instead
Keep the figure, because it comes from official facility records
Keep the figure but move it to an annex with a methods note
quiz.x: Routine data rarely proves attribution; contribution analysis explains how the programme plausibly contributed. Switching to training counts is the runner-up but retreats to activity measures and hides outcome evidence.

quiz.q: An M&E officer has 600 open-ended responses from community health workers in Cameroon's South West about barriers to referral. How can AI best help?
opts: Decide which barriers matter most and set the programme's priorities for next year
Translate the responses and delete the originals to save space
Replace the responses with a single summary score per district
Identify recurring themes, then the officer checks samples against text
quiz.x: AI surfaces themes across large qualitative datasets fast, with a person verifying against the raw text. Letting AI set priorities is the runner-up but hands an accountable decision to the tool.

quiz.q: A malaria programme's logframe lists 'training sessions held' and 'nets distributed' as its main success indicators. A donor reviewer is unhappy. What is the most likely reason?
opts: They are activity-level measures and show no change in outcomes
They are not specific enough to qualify as SMART indicators
They are outcome measures that should be listed as impact
They depend on DHIS2 data that is reported too slowly
quiz.x: Activities and outputs show the programme was busy; donors want outcomes such as net use. The SMART objection is the runner-up, but these indicators can be SMART yet still miss outcomes.

quiz.q: A regional store in Ngaoundere plans next quarter's vaccine orders using a forecast that matched actual use well last year. What ongoing practice does the module recommend?
opts: Let district managers override it whenever they disagree
Re-train the model each week on the newest daily data
Compare forecast with actual use each month and adjust
Lock the forecast for the year to keep ordering predictable
quiz.x: Forecasts should be compared with actual use each month and adjusted for stock-outs, seasonality and programme changes. Weekly re-training is the runner-up but adds noise and still lacks the human review against actuals.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian NGO drafts a Global Fund grant proposal with AI in two days instead of two weeks. The narrative cites coverage figures for the region. What is the essential step before submission?
opts: Shorten the narrative so reviewers see a concise proposal
Verify every figure against the source data and current reports
Add more figures so the proposal looks evidence-based
Have a second AI model polish the language and the structure
quiz.x: AI saves drafting time, but numbers must be verified; donors increasingly spot AI-polished reports with thin evidence. Polishing with a second model is the runner-up but improves style, not accuracy.

facts.t: Adjusted demand when a clinic used 300 units but was stocked out 10 of 30 days.
facts.more: 300 × 30 ÷ 20 = 450. Ordering on recorded consumption alone would repeat the stock-out.

facts.t: Open-source health information system, developed at the University of Oslo, used nationally in many countries.
facts.more: Completeness, timeliness and consistency of its data vary. Run data quality checks before any model or forecast.

facts.t: A logframe links activities → outputs → outcomes → impact.
facts.more: Donors increasingly reject reports that count activities but show no outcomes. AI can draft logframes fast — make the indicators honest.

facts.t: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound indicators.
facts.more: 'Improve health' is not an indicator; '% of children 12–23 months fully immunised in District X by December' is.

modules.d: The rules that make public health AI safe — privacy, fairness, transparency, and accountability.
modules.body:
The most important module: doing this right

Public health AI operates on the most sensitive data there is, at population scale, on behalf of people who often can't opt out. That combination makes governance non-negotiable. This module is the discipline that separates responsible public health AI from a data or equity disaster. Get the capability without this, and you have a liability; get both, and you have a genuine force for good.

Data protection: health data is special

  • Never expose identifiable data to non-approved tools. Patient and identifiable population data must only go to tools cleared under your institution's data-protection policy — never a random free chatbot. When in doubt, don't.
  • De-identify and minimize. Use the least identifiable data that answers the question; strip identifiers before any AI processing where possible.
  • Consent & purpose. Data collected for one purpose shouldn't be silently repurposed. Respect the basis on which it was gathered.
  • Know your legal framework. Data-protection laws vary by country (and many African nations now have specific ones); comply with yours, not just a global assumption.

Equity: AI can widen or narrow health gaps

  • Beware biased data. A model trained on data that under-represents your population may serve it badly — GIGO with life-and-death stakes. Ask "whose data built this, and who's missing?"
  • Access equity. AI tools that assume smartphones, connectivity, or one language can exclude the most vulnerable — the very people public health exists to serve. Design for inclusion.
  • Actively serve the underserved. Equity isn't neutrality; it's deliberately directing AI's benefits toward those with the least.

Transparency & accountability

  • Explainability: decisions affecting people should be explainable, not hidden in a black box. Prefer approaches you can justify.
  • Named human accountability: a person — not "the AI" — is responsible for each AI-informed decision.
  • Document & audit: record how AI was used and why, so decisions can be reviewed.
  • Human oversight throughout: AI informs; accountable professionals decide and can be questioned.
WHO's guidance on AI for health centers six principles — protecting autonomy; promoting human well-being and safety; ensuring transparency; fostering accountability; ensuring inclusiveness and equity; and promoting responsive, sustainable AI. Memorize the spirit: safe, fair, transparent, accountable, inclusive.
The public health AI governance test — before any deployment: ✓ identifiable data only in approved tools · ✓ data minimized/de-identified · ✓ the tool serves — not excludes — the vulnerable · ✓ checked for bias against your population · ✓ decisions explainable · ✓ a named human accountable · ✓ use documented. If you can't tick all seven, it's not ready.
🧪 Interactive Lab — Match the risk to its safeguard
Risk

🧪 Governance audit lab (copy → run on a real use case)

You are a public health AI governance advisor. Here is my intended AI use: [describe the tool, the data, the population, and the decision it informs]. Audit it against seven controls: (1) identifiable data only in approved tools, (2) data minimized/de-identified, (3) serves rather than excludes the vulnerable, (4) checked for bias against my population, (5) decisions explainable, (6) a named human accountable, (7) use documented. For each, tell me pass/fail and exactly what to fix. Then name the biggest equity risk and how to mitigate it.

Going deeper — frameworks for responsible public health AI

Several frameworks give structure to governance:

  • WHO's six principles for AI in health: protect autonomy; promote well-being, safety and the public interest; ensure transparency and explainability; foster responsibility and accountability; ensure inclusiveness and equity; and promote AI that is responsive and sustainable.
  • Africa: the African Union's Continental AI Strategy (2024) and the AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection (Malabo Convention, in force since 2023) shape regional expectations; national laws, such as Cameroon's 2024 personal data protection law, add obligations. Check implementation status in your country.
  • Data minimisation and purpose limitation: collect only what's needed, for a stated purpose, and keep it only as long as necessary.
  • Community engagement and data sovereignty: involve affected communities in decisions about how their data is used; consider where data is stored and who benefits from models built on it.
Algorithmic impact assessment. Before deployment, document: purpose, data sources, affected groups, potential harms (including to groups missing from the data), performance by subgroup, human oversight, appeal routes, and a review schedule. Re-run it when data or use changes.

Re-identification in aggregate data

Even aggregated tables can identify people when cells are small (e.g. one HIV-positive adolescent in a small village). Use thresholds, aggregation or statistical disclosure control before publishing.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a public health AI ethics adviser. For this proposed AI use [describe], conduct an algorithmic impact assessment: purpose, data sources and legal basis, affected and missing groups, potential harms, subgroup performance checks, human oversight, appeal routes, community engagement plan, and review schedule. Map it to WHO's six principles.

📚 Glossary

  • Purpose limitation: Using data only for the purpose it was collected for
  • Data minimisation: Collecting only data that's necessary
  • Algorithmic impact assessment: Structured review of an AI system's potential harms before use
  • Data sovereignty: The principle that data is subject to the laws and interests of the people and nation it comes from

📖 References

  • WHO (2021). Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health.
  • African Union (2024). Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy.
  • African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection (Malabo Convention).

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • When in doubt, don't. If you're unsure whether data can go into a tool, treat the answer as no until confirmed.
  • Equity is active, not neutral. Deliberately direct AI's benefits toward those with the least.
  • Name the accountable human. “The AI decided” is never an acceptable answer in public health.

📚 Glossary

  • De-identification: removing identifiers so data can't be traced to a person.
  • Data minimization: using the least data needed for the purpose.
  • Algorithmic bias: systematic unfairness from skewed data or design.
  • Explainability: being able to justify how a decision was reached.

📖 Explore further

  • WHO — Ethics & governance of AI for health.
  • Check your country's data-protection law and your institution's policy directly.

quiz.q: A district officer in Cameroon wants to paste a line list with patient names, phone numbers and HIV status into a free public chatbot to get a summary. The tool is not on the institution's approved list. What should he do?
opts: Remove the names but keep phone numbers so cases can be traced
Ask a colleague to do it from a personal account instead
Use an approved tool with de-identified data, or not proceed
Paste it, since the chatbot's privacy policy says chats are private
quiz.x: Identifiable health data must go only to approved tools, after minimisation and de-identification. Removing names is the runner-up but phone numbers still identify people, and the tool is still not approved.

quiz.q: An NPHI dashboard of HIV testing by village shows one village with a single positive adolescent. A programme officer wants to publish it because it is 'aggregate data'. What is the right decision?
opts: Suppress or aggregate small cells before it is published
Publish it with a note asking users to respect privacy
Share it with trusted partners on request in place of publishing
Publish it, since village totals do not name individuals
quiz.x: Small cells can re-identify people in small communities, so use thresholds, aggregation or disclosure control. Sharing with trusted partners is the runner-up but the re-identification risk remains.

quiz.q: A partner proposes using last year's household survey on water access to rank households for a nutrition programme. The survey consent covered water access. Which principle is most at stake?
opts: Explainability, since rankings may be hard to understand
Purpose limitation, as the data was gathered for another use
Data sovereignty, as the survey may be stored abroad
Data minimisation, since the survey had too many variables
quiz.x: Purpose limitation: data collected for one purpose should not be silently repurposed. Minimisation is the runner-up and also relevant, but the core problem is the change of purpose.

quiz.q: A vendor offers Cameroon's NPHI a 40% discount if it may use the institute's identifiable surveillance data to train its global model. What is the best response?
opts: Accept it, since the savings can fund more community testing
Accept it if the vendor signs a confidentiality agreement
Accept it after removing names, keeping all other fields
Decline it, unless purpose, consent, law and community allow it
quiz.x: This repurposes sensitive data without a lawful basis, consent or community engagement. A confidentiality agreement is the runner-up but does not fix purpose limitation or data sovereignty.

quiz.q: An AI tool for a Nigerian maternal health programme registers women by smartphone app in English. Rural women in the target area mostly use basic phones and speak Hausa. Which governance control fails?
opts: Data minimisation, as the app collects too much personal data
Accountability, as no named official runs the app
Access equity, as the design excludes the most vulnerable
Explainability, as women cannot see how the app decides
quiz.x: Tools that assume smartphones or one language exclude the very people public health serves. Explainability is a reasonable runner-up concern but the main failure is exclusion by design.

quiz.q: After an AI triage tool deprioritised a village for a nutrition survey, journalists ask who decided. The district manager says 'the system decided'. Which governance gap does this reveal?
opts: The model's training data under-represented that village
The vendor did not publish the model's source code
The data used in the triage was not fully de-identified
No named human was accountable for the AI-informed decision
quiz.x: A named person, not 'the AI', must be accountable for each AI-informed decision. Under-representation is the runner-up and may also be true, but the statement itself shows the accountability gap.

quiz.q: A Ministry of Health team in Cameroon asks which legal instruments to check before deploying an AI tool on personal health data. Which set best reflects the module?
opts: Cameroon's 2024 data protection law, plus the AU Malabo Convention
The EU GDPR, which governs all health data processed in Africa
WHO's six principles, which are binding law in member states
The AU AI Strategy alone, as it sets binding national rules
quiz.x: National law (Cameroon's 2024 personal data protection law) and the Malabo Convention (in force since 2023) shape obligations; check implementation status. The AU AI Strategy is the runner-up but it is a strategy, not binding national law; WHO principles are guidance.

quiz.q: An NPHI ran an algorithmic impact assessment on a TB screening tool last year. The tool is now being extended to children, using new paediatric data. What should happen?
opts: Ask the vendor to confirm the tool performs well in children
Re-run the assessment, as the data and use have changed
Rely on last year's assessment, since the tool is unchanged
Pilot in children and assess harms after six months of use
quiz.x: Impact assessments should be re-run when data or use changes, including subgroup performance checks. Piloting first is the runner-up but assesses harms after children are exposed.

quiz.q: A proposed AI tool passes six of the module's seven governance controls but has no documentation of how AI is used in decisions. The team wants to launch next week. What does the governance test say?
opts: Launch, then document within the first quarter of operation
Launch in one district while the documentation is drafted
Launch, as six of seven controls is a strong passing score
It is not ready until documentation of AI use is in place
quiz.x: The test is pass/fail: if you cannot tick all seven, it is not ready. A one-district launch is the runner-up but still deploys an undocumented, unauditable system.

quiz.q: A WHO-aligned review in Ethiopia asks whether an AI referral tool lets patients and clinicians understand and question its recommendations. Which WHO principle is this mainly testing?
opts: Ensuring inclusiveness and equity in use
Ensuring transparency and explainability
Promoting well-being, safety and the public interest
Promoting responsive and sustainable AI
quiz.x: Being able to understand and question recommendations is transparency and explainability. Accountability is close, but the question is about understanding the tool's reasoning rather than who answers for it.

facts.t: WHO principles for AI in health.
facts.more: Protect autonomy; promote well-being, safety and the public interest; ensure transparency; foster accountability; ensure inclusiveness and equity; promote responsive, sustainable AI.

facts.t: The AU Malabo Convention on cyber security and personal data protection entered into force.
facts.more: It shapes regional expectations alongside national laws. Check whether your own country has ratified and how it is implemented.

facts.t: The African Union adopted its Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy.
facts.more: It frames AI for development across Africa with attention to ethics, data and capacity. National policy follows at different speeds.

facts.t: The module's governance test before any deployment.
facts.more: Approved tools only, minimised data, serves the vulnerable, bias checked, explainable, a named accountable human, documented use. If you can't tick all seven, it's not ready.
