modules.t: Capstone: An Institutional AI Use Case
modules.d: Design a real, governed AI use case for your institution — valuable, safe, equitable, and accountable.
modules.body:
Prove you can bring AI to public health responsibly

Your capstone is a real, deployable AI use case for your institution — a concrete way AI will strengthen surveillance, analysis, communication, programs, or M&E, designed from the start to be safe, equitable, and accountable. This is the artifact that shows leadership you can capture AI's value and govern its risks — the exact combination public health needs. It's your qualification as a responsible public health AI practitioner.

Choose your use case

  • The Surveillance Enhancer: a workflow using AI to detect or summarize health signals faster from your available data sources.
  • The Analysis Accelerator: a rigorous, verified AI-assisted workflow for exploring data or synthesizing evidence for a real question.
  • The Communication System: an AI-assisted, human-reviewed pipeline for clear, multilingual, culturally-grounded health messaging at scale.
  • The Program/M&E Tool: an AI-supported workflow for planning, indicator tracking, qualitative analysis, or reporting.
  • Your own: any real, bounded, high-value use case for your institution.

Capstone requirements

  • Real and valuable — solves a genuine problem for your institution, not a hypothetical.
  • Clear on the human role — what AI does vs. what accountable professionals decide.
  • Passes the governance test — all seven controls from Module 4, with data protection and named accountability.
  • Equity-designed — shows how it serves rather than excludes the vulnerable, and is checked for bias.
  • Verified & rigorous — where it touches analysis or facts, it specifies what humans must verify.
  • Your prompt log — the CLEAR prompts used, with iterations, proving the skill.
  • A short reflection — the value it delivers, the risks it manages, and where human judgment stays central.
"The goal is not AI in public health — it's better public health, with AI as one powerful tool held in responsible hands." Your capstone is that sentence made real: measurable value, governed carefully, serving everyone — especially those with the least.
🎓 Certification. Passing every module (75%+) and completing your governed capstone earns the AI Unlocked: Public Health certificate — a print-ready PDF with a QR validation code, signed by Innocent Forteh, Program Director, Team21 Academy. Each module also carries its own certificate in your Certificates tab.
Lead onward. Extend this with Level 2 OPERATE (build the automations and systems behind your use case), the NGOs & Nonprofits or Procurement specializations (programs and supply chains), or Executive Leadership (lead your institution's AI adoption). Public health needs practitioners who are both capable and principled — you're becoming one.
🧪 Capstone planner (copy → run to design your use case)

You are my capstone advisor for a public health AI use case at my institution: [describe the institution, its mandate, and a real problem]. Help me choose the strongest use case (surveillance, analysis, communication, or program/M&E). Then design it: what AI does vs what accountable humans decide, how it passes all seven governance controls (data protection, bias check, equity, explainability, named accountability, documentation), what must be human-verified, and how it serves the most vulnerable. Finish with exactly what my finished submission must contain and a realistic first-step plan.

🧪 Validated exercise

The real goal isn't 'AI in public health' — it's better public health, with AI as a tool in responsible ___.

Going deeper — making your use case fundable and approvable

Leaders approve use cases that are specific, measured, safe and affordable to sustain. Strengthen your capstone with:

  • Problem statement with numbers: "District reports arrive an average of 12 days late; outbreak responses start late as a result" beats "reporting is slow".
  • Theory of change: if we do X, then Y happens, leading to Z — with assumptions stated.
  • Phased plan: pilot in one or two districts, evaluate against a baseline, then scale with go/no-go criteria.
  • Total cost of ownership: licences or compute, connectivity, training, maintenance, data management staff, and governance time — not just the tool price. Many pilots fail at scale because recurring costs were never budgeted.
  • Sustainability and ownership: who runs it after the pilot, and how does it fit national systems (e.g. DHIS2) rather than creating a parallel one?
Pilot metrics. Choose 3–5: a process measure (reports on time), an output (alerts verified within 48 hours), an outcome (time from signal to response), an equity measure (performance across districts), and a safety measure (false alerts, privacy incidents).
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a health systems funding reviewer. Here is my AI use case draft: [paste]. Strengthen the problem statement with numbers, write a theory of change with assumptions, design a phased pilot with go/no-go criteria, estimate total cost of ownership for three years, and propose 3–5 pilot metrics including equity and safety.

📚 Glossary

  • Theory of change: Explanation of how activities lead to intended outcomes
  • Total cost of ownership: All costs over a system's lifetime, not just purchase
  • Go/no-go criteria: Pre-agreed conditions for scaling or stopping
  • Parallel system: A separate system duplicating an existing national one

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Build what your institution will use. A real, bounded use case beats an ambitious hypothetical.
  • Governance is graded. The seven-point test and equity design are requirements, not extras.
  • Your prompt log proves the skill. Document the CLEAR prompts and iterations behind the work.

📚 Glossary

  • Use case: a specific, real application of AI to a problem.
  • Governance test: the seven-control check from Module 4.
  • Capstone: the real, governed use case that completes the course.

📖 Explore further

  • Continue with Level 2, the NGO/Procurement specializations, or Executive Leadership.
  • Share your capstone with the Team21 community — team21online@gmail.com.

quiz.q: A capstone draft for the Far North regional delegation states: 'Reporting is slow, so we will use AI.' A reviewer asks for a stronger problem statement. Which rewrite best meets the module's standard?
opts: AI could help modernise reporting for the whole region
Reporting is slow and staff are frustrated with current tools
Weekly reports arrive 12 days late, so responses start late
Reporting is a widely recognised challenge across Africa
quiz.x: Strong problem statements use numbers and link them to consequences. The frustration statement is the runner-up because it names a real issue, but it gives no measure to evaluate against.

quiz.q: A capstone plans AI-flagged anomalies in DHIS2 data for a 10-district pilot. Which metric is the best example of an outcome measure, as the module defines pilot metrics?
opts: Days from signal to response by the district
Number of alerts verified within 48 hours
Number of false alerts and privacy incidents
Percentage of district reports submitted on time
quiz.x: Time from signal to response is the outcome. Alerts verified within 48 hours is the runner-up but is an output; reports on time is a process measure; false alerts is a safety measure.

quiz.q: A team budgets a 3-year AI pilot: licence $6,000 a year, connectivity $2,400 a year, one-off training $3,000, and maintenance $1,500 a year. What is the 3-year total cost of ownership?
opts: $12,900, counting each cost once
$29,700, leaving out the training
$32,700, including all four items
$38,700, counting training each year
quiz.x: (6,000 + 2,400 + 1,500) x 3 + 3,000 = 32,700. Counting training each year ($38,700) is the runner-up error, since training is a one-off cost here.

quiz.q: A capstone proposes a new stand-alone AI surveillance database for a region that already reports through DHIS2. What is the strongest reviewer concern?
opts: It creates a parallel system and weakens sustainability
Its interface may not match regional staff preferences
Its vendor may not support French-language interfaces
Its data model may be too large for the region's servers
quiz.x: Use cases should fit national systems such as DHIS2 rather than create a parallel one. Server capacity is the runner-up technical worry but secondary to the sustainability problem.

quiz.q: A capstone pilot ran in two districts. Signal-to-response time fell from 9 to 6 days, but false alerts tripled and one privacy incident occurred. Go/no-go criteria included 'no privacy incidents'. What should happen?
opts: Scale it, because the main outcome improved by a third
Pause scaling, fix the causes and re-evaluate against criteria
Drop the privacy criterion, since one incident is a small rate
Scale it to two more districts to gather more evidence
quiz.x: Pre-agreed go/no-go criteria exist to stop scaling when safety conditions fail. Expanding to two more districts is the runner-up but spreads a known privacy risk.

quiz.q: A capstone submission describes a strong use case, a governance check and a pilot plan, but no record of the prompts used. What requirement is missing?
opts: A reflection on value, risks and human judgment
An equity check by district and population subgroup
A theory of change with the assumptions stated
A prompt log of CLEAR prompts and their iterations
quiz.x: The prompt log proves the skill and is a stated requirement. A theory of change is the runner-up as a strengthening element, but the scenario names the missing prompts.

quiz.q: A capstone for a Cameroonian NPHI uses AI to draft weekly epidemiological bulletins. Which statement best defines the human role for this use case?
opts: AI writes and sends bulletins; staff review a sample monthly
Staff write bulletins; AI checks their spelling and grammar
AI drafts; the comms officer edits the tone before release
AI drafts; the epidemiologist verifies figures and approves
quiz.x: The accountable epidemiologist must verify figures and approve before release. Comms tone editing is the runner-up, but it does not verify epidemiological facts.

quiz.q: Two capstone options are proposed: an ambitious national AI early-warning platform, or AI-assisted cleaning of weekly malaria data in one region. Which does the module favour, and why?
opts: Neither, until the institution has a full AI governance office
The national platform, because it has the greatest potential reach
The regional cleaning workflow, as it is real, bounded and usable
The national platform, if a donor will fund its first two years
quiz.x: The module favours a real, bounded use case the institution will use over an ambitious hypothetical. Donor-funded national scale is the runner-up but risks unbudgeted recurring costs.

quiz.q: A capstone's equity section says: 'The tool is neutral and treats all districts the same.' What would make it meet the module's standard?
opts: Checking performance by district and directing benefits to the worst-off
Applying the tool first in the best-connected districts for speed
Removing any district names so the tool cannot discriminate
Adding a statement that the vendor's model was tested for bias
quiz.x: Equity is active, not neutral: check subgroup performance and deliberately serve the underserved. A vendor bias statement is the runner-up but is not a check on your own population.

quiz.q: A capstone pilot plan lists: record a baseline, run the pilot, then do the governance test after the first month. What is wrong with the sequence?
opts: The theory of change should be written after evaluation
The governance test should come before the pilot starts
The pilot should run across the whole region from the very start
The baseline should be recorded after the pilot has ended
quiz.x: Governance comes before the pilot, not after the first incident. Moving the baseline is a sequencing error but a lesser one; a baseline belongs before the pilot.

facts.t: Pass mark on every module for the AI Unlocked: Public Health certificate.
facts.more: Plus a governed capstone use case that passes all seven controls from Module 4.

facts.t: Pilot metrics to choose: process, output, outcome, equity and safety.
facts.more: For example: reports on time; alerts verified within 48 hours; time from signal to response; performance across districts; false alerts and privacy incidents.

facts.t: Total cost of ownership: licences, connectivity, training, maintenance, data staff, governance time.
facts.more: Many pilots fail at scale because recurring costs were never budgeted. Estimate at least three years.

facts.t: Build into national systems such as DHIS2, not alongside them.
facts.more: Parallel systems split data, double staff workload and die when the project ends. Plan who runs it after the pilot.
